result:
The proposed answer is incorrect, because its optimization rests on a flawed first-order approximation.

**Bowtie count in G_q.** In K^q_{⌈n/2⌉,⌊n/2⌋}, all triangles consist of one added edge in A together with a vertex of B. A bowtie needs two triangles sharing exactly one vertex. A center in B works with any two of the q disjoint added edges, which gives ⌊n/2⌋·C(q,2) bowties. A center in A gives none, since each A-vertex has at most one A-neighbor and no B–B edges exist. So G_q has ⌊n/2⌋·q(q−1)/2 bowties, which is about nq²/4.

**Flaw in the proposed reasoning.** The solution assumes the spectral radius is additive to first order, so that edges can be moved to the other part at no cost. The increase in λ is only matched to first order, though. The second-order behavior favors concentrating all the added edges in one part: λ is convex-like in this perturbation, so splitting the edges between the two parts gives a strictly smaller spectral radius than G_q. A split graph therefore does not satisfy λ(G) ≥ λ(G_q). The proposed constraint q_A/a + q_B/b ≈ q/a is also internally inconsistent, since it treats B-edges as worth more while the true first-order gains are essentially equal. The claimed halving to nq²/8 therefore does not hold.

I did not verify the extremal theorem rigorously. I am relying on the second-order convexity argument and my recollection that the known result is that G_q's bowtie count is the minimum, namely ⌊n/2⌋·q(q−1)/2. The proposed nq²/8 differs from this by roughly a factor of 2 at leading order, so it is wrong.

VERDICT: REJECT
